record.paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
record.original_question: How can genetic studies understand, prevent, and correct selection bias or collider bias when voluntary participation, separate case-control recruitment, or survival among cases makes sampled cohorts unrepresentative and can induce spurious genetic associations or biased SNP-heritability estimates?

evidence.quote: Selection bias describes a situation where a study cohort does not perfectly represent the population that it is presumed to represent, leading to unjustified conclusions about the general population.

Since the problem of selection bias in genetic studies was acknowledged only recently, not enough work has been dedicated to fully understanding the scope of the problem and working out methods and best practices to minimize its effect (open problem #9: selection bias).
the common case-control study design (where cases and controls are recruited separately) can lead to underestimation of SNP heritability, thereby adding to the missing heritability

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a population $\mathcal{P}$ of individuals, each characterized by a genotype vector $G \in \{0,1,2\}^M$ (counts of a reference allele at $M$ single-nucleotide polymorphisms, SNPs) and a phenotype $Y$ (either quantitative or a binary case/control status). A genome-wide association study (GWAS) seeks to estimate, for each SNP $j$, the marginal effect $\beta_j$ in a model $Y = \sum_j G_j \beta_j + \varepsilon$, while the SNP-heritability is defined as $h^2_{\text{SNP}} = \mathrm{Var}\!\left(\sum_j G_j \beta_j\right)/\mathrm{Var}(Y)$ (with an appropriate liability-scale transformation in the binary case).

Suppose that the actually observed cohort is not a simple random sample from $\mathcal{P}$ but is drawn according to a sampling indicator $S \in \{0,1\}$ whose distribution depends on $Y$, on $G$, and on unobserved covariates $U$. Three concrete mechanisms are of interest:
(i) voluntary participation, where $\Pr(S=1 \mid Y, G, U)$ depends on health, behavior, or socio-demographic variables correlated with $Y$ and $G$;
(ii) separate case/control ascertainment, where cases ($Y=1$) and controls ($Y=0$) are recruited from different source populations with different distributions of $G$ and $U$;
(iii) survival/prevalence sampling, where among cases only survivors are observed, so that $\Pr(S=1 \mid Y=1, G, U)$ depends on genetic and environmental modifiers of survival.

Conditioning on $S=1$ can open non-causal paths between $G$ and $Y$ (collider bias), producing spurious association signals at SNPs that are not causal, and can systematically distort estimates of $h^2_{\text{SNP}}$ and of genetic correlations between traits.

Develop a rigorous framework that accomplishes all of the following:
(a) Characterize, under explicit and testable assumptions on the selection mechanism $\Pr(S=1 \mid Y, G, U)$, the bias induced in marginal SNP effect estimates $\hat\beta_j$ and in SNP-heritability estimates $\hat h^2_{\text{SNP}}$ obtained from the selected sample.
(b) Provide consistent estimation procedures (using, e.g., external population information, instrumental variables, inverse probability weighting, or auxiliary unselected reference panels) that recover the population-level $\beta_j$ and $h^2_{\text{SNP}}$ from cohorts subject to mechanisms (i)–(iii), together with conditions under which identifiability holds.
(c) Establish best-practice study-design and analysis guidelines (recruitment schemes, weighting, sensitivity analyses) that provably minimize or bound the residual bias when the selection mechanism is only partially known.
artifact.category_tag: selection bias in genetic association studies
artifact.status_search_result: Several partial solutions have appeared: the PCGC approach estimates SNP-heritability and genetic correlations in case-control studies under non-genetic risk factors; Slope-Hunter and Mendelian-randomization-based estimators correct collider bias in conditional GWAS; and inverse-probability-weighted GWAS (WGWAS) corrects volunteer bias and recovers larger SNP effect sizes and heritability. However, no single framework simultaneously handles voluntary participation, separate case-control ascertainment, and survival bias under weak assumptions, so the broader problem remains active research.

status_evidence.title: Correcting for volunteer bias in GWAS increases SNP effect sizes and heritability estimates
status_evidence.snippet: Inverse probability weighted GWAS (WGWAS) can correct GWAS summary statistics for volunteer bias.
status_evidence.claim: Volunteer-bias correction methods exist and increase recovered SNP effect sizes and heritability.

status_evidence.title: A robust method for collider bias correction in conditional genome-wide association studies
status_evidence.snippet: Slope-Hunter uses model-based clustering to correct collider bias, even in the presence of genetic correlation.
status_evidence.claim: Collider bias in conditional GWAS has partial methodological solutions.

status_evidence.title: Estimating SNP-Based Heritability and Genetic Correlation in Case-Control Studies Directly and with Summary Statistics
status_evidence.snippet: PCGC is the only method that can estimate both SNP-based heritability and genetic correlation accurately in the presence of important non-genetic risk factors.
status_evidence.claim: Case-control SNP-heritability estimation has been partially addressed via PCGC.

status_evidence.title: Collider bias correction for multiple covariates in GWAS using robust multivariable Mendelian randomization
status_evidence.snippet: Approaches have been developed to correct collider bias through Mendelian randomization.
status_evidence.claim: Multiple methods exist but a unified framework remains incomplete.
